# Antiplatelet agents

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Relevant pharmacology > Antiplatelet agents*

[Original Article Link](/library/Um0bUg)

---

## Summary

Antiplatelet agents are drugs that inhibit enzymes or <u>receptors</u> required for <u>platelet activation</u>, <u>platelet aggregation</u>, and/or <u>thrombus formation</u>. The most commonly used antiplatelet agent is <u>acetylsalicylic acid</u> (<u>aspirin</u>), which is an irreversible <u>cyclooxygenase</u> inhibitor with dose-dependent antiplatelet, <u>antipyretic</u>, <u>analgesic</u>, and antiinflammatory actions. <u>Low-dose aspirin</u> is used in the management of cardiovascular events (e.g., acute <u>MI</u>) and for primary/secondary prophylaxis of cardiovascular disease. Adverse effects of <u>aspirin</u> include <u>peptic ulcers</u>, hemorrhage, <u>salicylate toxicity</u>, <u>aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease</u>, and <u>Reye syndrome</u>. <u>P2Y12 receptor antagonists</u> (<u>clopidogrel</u>, <u>prasugrel</u>, <u>ticagrelor</u>) are mainly used in conjunction with <u>aspirin</u> (<u>dual antiplatelet therapy</u>) in the <u>management of acute coronary syndrome</u> and to prevent <u>stent thrombosis</u> in patients after <u>percutaneous coronary intervention</u> (<u>PCI</u>). Although <u>allergic reactions</u> are more common, <u>P2Y12 receptor antagonists</u> cause fewer hemorrhagic/gastrointestinal complications compared to <u>aspirin</u>. <u>Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors</u> (<u>abciximab</u>, <u>eptifibatide</u>, and <u>tirofiban</u>) are parenterally administered, rapid-acting antiplatelet agents that are only used in high-risk patients in which <u>PCI</u> is planned. <u>Gp IIb/IIIa</u> inhibitors can cause a sudden drop in <u>platelet counts</u> (acute profound <u>thrombocytopenia</u>), necessitating <u>platelet count</u> monitoring. All antiplatelet agents increase the risk of hemorrhage and are usually contraindicated in patients who have <u>thrombocytopenia</u> or active/recent bleeding (e.g., <u>hemorrhagic stroke</u>, major <u>surgery</u> within the past 30 days).

## Irreversible cyclooxygenase inhibitors

### Agents [[1]](/library/Qw0uiR)




<u>Acetylsalicylic acid</u> (<u>ASA</u>, <u>aspirin</u>)




### Mechanism of action [[2]](/library/Pw0WQR)[[3]](/library/4w03QR)




<u>ASA</u> covalently attaches an acetyl group to <u>COX</u>.




* Irreversible <u>COX-1</u> inhibition → inhibition of thromboxane (<u>TXA2</u>) synthesis in <u>platelets</u> → inhibition of <u>platelet aggregation</u> (antithrombotic effect)

* Onset of antiplatelet action: within minutes

* Duration of antiplatelet action: 7–10 days

* Irreversible <u>COX-1</u> and <u>COX-2</u> inhibition → inhibition of <u>prostacyclin</u> and <u>prostaglandin</u> synthesis → <u>antipyretic</u>, anti-inflammatory, and <u>analgesic</u> effect





### Effects




* Low dose (below 300 mg/day): inhibition of <u>platelet aggregation</u>

* Intermediate dose (300-2400 mg/day): <u>antipyretic</u> and <u>analgesic</u> effect

* High dose (2400-4000 mg/day): antiinflammatory effect





### Indications




* Acute <u>myocardial infarction</u>

* Acute <u>ischemic stroke</u> [[4]](/library/dMYonp)

* <u>Angina</u> (stable and unstable)

* <u>Management of ASCVD</u>

* <u>Primary prevention of ASCVD</u> and <u>colorectal cancer</u>  [[5]](/library/Ow0IQR)

* Symptomatic <u>peripheral arterial disease</u>

* <u>Giant cell arteritis</u>

* Prevention of <u>stent thrombosis</u> after <u>revascularization</u> procedures (e.g., <u>PTCA</u>, <u>CABG</u>, <u>carotid endarterectomy</u>)

* See “<u>Non-opioid analgesics</u>” for indications in <u>pain management</u> and inflammation.





### Adverse effects




* Gastrointestinal (most common): <u>aspirin</u> blocks <u>COX-1</u> → inhibition of conversion <u>arachidonic acid</u> to <u>PGH2</u> → ↓ formation of <u>PGE2</u> ;  → ↓ secretion of mucus and <u>bicarbonate</u> by <u>epithelium</u> → loss of protective layer on <u>mucosa</u> → <u>gastric acid</u> damages tissue → ↑ risk of <u>ulcers</u>, bleeding, and perforation 

* <u>Dyspepsia</u>

* Gastric <u>ulceration</u>, hemorrhage, perforation

* <u>Coagulopathy</u> and bleeding: These effects continue until new <u>platelets</u> are formed.

* ↑ <u>Bleeding time</u>

* <u>Prothrombin time</u> (<u>PT</u>) and <u>partial thromboplastin time</u> (<u>PTT</u>) are not affected.

* <u>Tinnitus</u>: <u>aspirin</u> affects the <u>vestibulocochlear nerve</u>

* Renal (in the case of long-term use)

* <u>Acute kidney injury</u>

* <u>Acute interstitial nephritis</u>

* <u>Salicylate poisoning</u>: See “<u>Salicylate toxicity</u>.

* <u>Allergic reactions</u>

* Cutaneous reactions

* <u>Anaphylactoid reactions</u>





### Contraindications




* <u>Febrile</u> illness in individuals < 19 years of age

* <u>Acute gout</u> attack  [[6]](/library/RSYlzo)





### Complications




* <u>Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease</u>; see “<u>NSAID hypersensitivity</u>.”

* <u>Reye syndrome</u>





#### Reye syndrome [[7]](/library/ow00PR)[[8]](/library/Kw0UPR)




* Description: a rare type of <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u> that is associated with <u>aspirin</u> use for viral illness in children < 19 years

* Etiology: <u>aspirin</u> use in individuals < 19 years of age with a <u>febrile</u> illness  [[9]](/library/pw0LPR)[[10]](/library/ipXJ6_)

* Pathophysiology [[11]](/library/Jw0sPR)

* <u>Viruses</u> alter the metabolism of <u>salicylates</u>  → accumulation of <u>salicylate</u> metabolites in the <u>liver</u> → <u>mitochondrial</u> injury and reversible inhibition of enzymes required for <u>fatty acid oxidation</u>;  → failure of hepatic <u>ATP</u> production → <u>acute hepatic failure</u> → <u>hyperammonemia</u>, <u>metabolic acidosis</u>, and <u>hepatic steatosis</u> → <u>acute encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Hyperammonemia</u> → <u>cerebral edema</u> → ↑ <u>ICP</u>

* Clinical features

* Preceding viral infection (e.g., <u>influenza</u>, <u>varicella</u> or <u>viral gastroenteritis</u>): The first symptoms of <u>Reye syndrome</u> usually begin 3–5 days after a viral illness.

* <u>Acute encephalopathy</u>

* Severe <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>;  (ranging from <u>lethargy</u> to <u>delirium</u> and <u>coma</u>)

* Neurological symptoms (e.g., <u>seizures</u>, <u>fixed pupils</u>)

* <u>Liver</u> failure

* Fatty degeneration

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>; further testing to rule out other causes (diagnosis of exclusion)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* ↑ <u>AST</u> and <u>ALT</u>

* <u>Hyperammonemia</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u>

* Prolonged <u>INR</u>

* <u>Cranial</u> CT/<u>MRI</u>: may show <u>cerebral edema</u> and scattered lesions

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> and <u>CSF analysis</u>: <u>WBC</u> < 8/Î¼L

* <u>Liver biopsy</u>: microvesicular <u>hepatic steatosis</u>

* Treatment: supportive

* Decrease <u>intracranial pressure</u> (e.g., via <u>osmotic diuresis</u>; elevation of the head)

* Correction of <u>hypoglycemia</u>

* Cardiopulmonary support if necessary

* Complications

* <u>Renal failure</u>

* Cardiac failure

* Prevention

* <u>Aspirin</u> should be avoided in individuals < 19 years of age, especially those with <u>fever</u>.

* Exception: children with <u>Kawasaki disease</u>

* Prognosis

* Outcomes vary from complete recovery to permanent neurological deficits.

* Increased <u>morbidity</u> and <u>mortality rate</u>  [[7]](/library/ow00PR)





> [!TIP]
> The lifespan of a <u>platelet</u> is 7–10 days. If <u>aspirin</u> is held prior to <u>surgery</u>, it should be discontinued one week in advance.




> [!TIP]
> Emergency correction of the antiplatelet effect of <u>aspirin</u> can only be achieved by administering <u>platelet</u> concentrates.




> [!NOTE]
> To memorize the symptoms of <u>Reye syndrome</u>, remember that “It’s never Rainy (Reye) in CHILE”: Coma, Hepatomegaly/Hypoglycemia, history of viral Infection, Liver failure, Encephalopathy.

## P2Y12 receptor antagonists

### Agents [[12]](/library/7w044R)[[13]](/library/Dw01OR)




* Clopidogrel

* Pro-drug

* Activation is dependent on hepatic cytochrome P enzymes.

* Not effective in individuals with genetic <u>polymorphisms</u> of <u>CYP</u> enzymes or drug-induced inhibition of <u>CYP</u> enzymes (e.g., <u>cimetidine</u>, <u>amiodarone</u>, <u>omeprazole</u>, etc.)

* Prasugrel

* Pro-drug

* Faster acting and more potent than <u>clopidogrel</u>

* Ticagrelor

* Not a pro-drug

* Orally administered direct <u>antagonist</u> of P2Y12 <u>platelet</u> <u>receptor</u>

* Faster acting and more potent than <u>clopidogrel</u>

* Ticlopidine: irreversible <u>P2Y12 receptor antagonist</u>

* Cangrelor: IV administered <u>P2Y12 receptor antagonist</u>





### Mechanism of action



* Inhibition of P2Y12 <u>receptor</u> on <u>platelets</u> (<u>ADP</u> <u>receptor</u>) → ↓ expression of <u>Gp IIb/IIIa</u> <u>receptors</u> on <u>platelets</u> → inhibition of <u>platelet aggregation</u>

* <u>ADP</u> usually binds to P2Y12 <u>receptors</u>, leading to activation of <u>Gp IIb/IIIa</u> <u>receptors</u> and subsequent <u>platelet aggregation</u>.

* <u>Irreversible inhibition</u>: <u>clopidogrel</u>, <u>prasugrel</u>, <u>ticlopidine</u>

* Reversible inhibition: <u>ticagrelor</u>




### Indications




* <u>Dual antiplatelet therapy</u> (in combination with <u>acetylsalicylic acid</u>)

* <u>STEMI</u>

* <u>Unstable angina</u>/<u>NSTEMI</u>

* <u>Secondary prevention</u> of cardiac events in patients post <u>PCI</u> and/or <u>stenting</u>

* Before <u>PCI</u>

* Alternative to <u>aspirin</u> in cases of intolerance: to prevent recurrence of <u>thromboembolic events</u>, including <u>ischemic stroke</u>, <u>MI</u>, and symptomatic <u>peripheral arterial disease</u>





### Adverse effects




* <u>Allergic reactions</u> (<u>rash</u>, <u>pruritus</u>, <u>anaphylaxis</u>)

* Hemorrhage

* Gastrointestinal upset

* Possibly <u>TTP</u>

* <u>Ticlopidine</u>: <u>neutropenia</u>/<u>agranulocytosis</u>

---

## Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors

### Agents




* Abciximab (<u>Fab region</u> fragments of <u>monoclonal antibodies</u> against <u>glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors</u>)

* Eptifibatide

* Tirofiban [[14]](/library/Z90ZNR)





### Mechanism of action [[15]](/library/Cw0qOR)



* <u>Gp IIb/IIIa</u> inhibitors bind to and block <u>glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors</u> (<u>fibrinogen</u> <u>receptor</u>) on the surface of activated <u>platelets</u> → prevention of <u>platelets</u> binding to <u>fibrinogen</u>;   → inhibition of <u>platelet aggregation</u> and <u>thrombus formation</u>




### Indication [[16]](/library/9w0NOR)



* Prevention of <u>thrombotic</u> complications in high-risk patients with <u>unstable angina</u>/<u>NSTEMI</u> planned for <u>PCI</u> within 24 hours




### Adverse effects




* Acute profound <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* Hemorrhage





> [!NOTE]
> To remember that <u>ABC</u>iximab targets glycoproteins IIb/IIIa, think <u>ABC</u> rhymes with 123!




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Abciximab</u> and <u>tirofiban</u> are contraindicated in patients with <u>thrombocytes</u> < 100,000/mmÂ³!




> [!NOTE]
> Eptifibatide and tirofiban are fibrinogen <u>receptor</u> blockers.

---

## Contraindications

* <u>Allergy</u>

* Active/recent bleeding within the past 30 days (e.g., <u>gastric ulcers</u>, <u>intracranial bleeding</u>)

* Major <u>surgery</u>/severe trauma within the past 30 days

* Severe <u>hypertension</u>

* <u>Aortic dissection</u>

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u>




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---
